inline.s: However, one must not become arrogant and self-satisfied over this, or stand still in one's tracks. In the past, Master Qu Boyu worked extremely hard at correcting his faults. At the age of twenty, he thought he had already corrected all the faults and evils of the past. By twenty-one, he realized that at twenty he had not yet finished correcting them. At twenty-two, looking back on his twenty-first year, he realized that during that period he had still been muddled, and the faults he ought to have corrected were not yet corrected. But he persisted steadfastly, year after year, each year improving upon the foundation of the previous one. Even at age fifty, he still knew that at forty-nine there were places where his correction had not been thorough. So diligent was the ancients' learning of correcting their faults! We are all in the class of ordinary people, and our many faults and evils cluster upon us like the quills of a hedgehog; yet when we look back on the past, we often see no faults at all — this is entirely due to carelessness, our eyes blinded by selfishness and desire.

However, those whose faults and evils are deep and heavy also show signs: sometimes the mind is dull and blocked, forgetting as soon as one turns one's head; sometimes one is troubled for no reason; or upon seeing a person of lofty virtue, one feels ashamed and downcast; or upon hearing proper and upright speech, one is displeased; or when one does others good, one instead draws their resentment; or one often has bad dreams, even speaks wildly, and loses the spirit of being human — all these are the appearance of having done evil. If such phenomena occur, one must certainly stir oneself to effort, and before the disaster arrives, discard the old and seek the new, cut off evil and cultivate good — by all means do not delude yourself!

blocks.text: Part Three: The Way of Accumulating Good

inline.s: The Classic of Changes says: "A household that accumulates good is sure to have an abundance of blessings left to bequeath to its descendants." In the past, when the Yan family was considering giving their daughter in marriage to Confucius' father, they recounted at length the long accumulation of virtue in his ancestors, and thereby foresaw that his descendants would surely flourish. Confucius praised Shun as a great filial son, saying: "Because of the utmost sincerity of his filial heart, when he sacrificed to his ancestors in the ancestral temple he moved them to come and receive the offering; his virtue and blessings are deep, and his descendants, generation after generation, will pass them on." These are all exceedingly accurate and profound judgments; now I will use events that have already happened in the past to verify and prove them.

Yang Rong, who rose to the rank of Junior Tutor, was a man of Jianning Prefecture, whose family for generations had made their living by ferrying a boat. Because of a torrential rain that lasted days on end, the river swelled high, the floodwaters destroyed the dwellings of the residents, and the drowned drifted downstream. The other boats were all busy salvaging the goods, but only Yang Rong's great-grandfather and grandfather were busy rescuing people, taking nothing of the drifting goods. The people of the village all mocked them as foolish.

By the time Yang Rong's father was born, the family's circumstances had gradually grown comfortable. A supernatural being, appearing in the form of a Daoist, said to Yang Rong's father: "Because your grandfather and father have hidden virtue, their descendants will become great officials, wealthy and honored. You should bury them in such-and-such a place; the feng shui there is very good." Thereupon Yang Rong's father buried his grandfather and father at the place the Daoist indicated. This tomb is now famous; it is what people call the White Rabbit Tomb.

Later Yang Rong was born. At twenty he passed the highest examination and rose in office to the Three Dukes; the emperor even conferred upon his great-grandfather, grandfather, and father the same official rank as his own. His descendants are honored and numerous, and to this day there are still many among them of virtue and ability.

Yang Zicheng of Yin County was at first a clerk in the county magistrate's office. His heart was kind and generous, and he observed the law with fairness. At that time the magistrate was very stern and severe. Once he ordered an attendant to beat a prisoner until blood flowed all over the ground, yet he was still angry without cease, and even commanded another beating. Yang Zicheng, seeing this, was deeply distressed, and knelt down to plead for mercy on the prisoner's behalf. The magistrate said, "With your intercession, I could well pardon him; but this man, having broken the law, still argues stubbornly — it is impossible not to be angered." Yang Zicheng kowtowed and said, "The corruption and tyranny of those in office, and the scattering of the people's hearts, has lasted long. When a case is examined and the truth is obtained, one ought to grieve for those involved and pity them — by no means rejoice and be pleased, lest one misjudge. If one must not even rejoice, how much less should one be angry? For under anger, it is very easy to extort a confession by torture!" Hearing Yang Zicheng's words, the magistrate was deeply moved and so let his anger subside.

Yang Zicheng's family was extremely poor. Because the position in the yamen carried a good deal of power, many people came to give gifts, but he refused them all. Whenever prisoners in the jail had nothing to eat, he would always find some way to relieve them. One day several new prisoners arrived with nothing to eat, and his own household was short of rice. If he gave the little rice the family had to the prisoners, then his own family would have nothing to eat; if he ate it himself, then the prisoners would be pitifully starving. So Yang Zicheng discussed it with his wife. His wife asked him, "Where do these prisoners come from?" He replied, "They come from Hangzhou. Along the way they had nothing to eat, enduring hunger to make it here, their faces all sallow." Thereupon husband and wife took out the rice they had been waiting to eat, cooked it into congee, and gave it to the prisoners.

Later two sons were born: the elder, Yang Shouchen, and the younger, Yang Shouzhi. One became Vice Minister of Personnel in Nanjing, the other Vice Minister of Personnel in Beijing. The eldest grandson rose to Vice Minister of Justice, and the second grandson became the Corruption Commissioner of Sichuan. These four men were all renowned officials. Yang Chuting and Yang Dezheng, whom we know today, are both descendants of Yang Zicheng.

In the past, during the Zhengtong era, Deng Maoqi rebelled in Fujian, and many scholars and common people followed him. The court appointed Zhang Kai of Yin County, who had once served as Censor-in-Chief, to lead troops south to Fujian to suppress the rebellion, and by stratagem he captured Deng Maoqi. Later Zhang Kai commissioned a Director of Affairs surnamed Xie under the Fujian Provincial Administration Commission to search out and seize the remnants in the eastern part of Fujian, ordering him to kill any he caught.

Director Xie would not slaughter the innocent indiscriminately, so he found a way to obtain the register of those who had attached themselves to Deng Maoqi. To every person not named in the register he secretly gave a small white cloth flag, and told him: on the day the government troops arrive, plant this white flag at your door. At the same time he strictly forbade the soldiers: no household that has planted a white flag may be killed arbitrarily. In this way more than ten thousand people were saved.
Later Director Xie's son, Xie Qian, took first place in the highest examinations and rose to the office of Grand Chancellor; his grandson Xie Pi also took third place.

In the Lin family of Putian County, Fujian, there was an elderly woman of the older generation who loved to do good. She often gave rice-flour dumplings to the poor. Whenever someone came asking, she would give them at once, never with a look of weariness. A transcendent being, appearing as a Daoist, came every morning to ask for six or seven dumplings. The old woman gave them to him every day, the same for three years without a hint of impatience. Thereupon the transcendent knew that her good deeds came from a heart of utmost sincerity. So he said to her, "I have eaten your dumplings for three years; how should I repay you? Behind your house there is a plot of land. If you are buried there, your descendants who become officials and are enfeoffed will be as many as the seeds in a liter of sesame." When she died, her son, following the place indicated, buried her there. In the first generation alone nine people passed the highest examinations, and afterwards many of every generation held great office — so much so that in Fujian there is a folk rhyme: "Without the Lins no list is opened; when the list is opened, the Lins are surely there."

Grand Historian Feng, whose name was Qi and whose courtesy name was Zhuo'an — in those days his father was a student at the county school. Rising early one bitterly cold winter day to go to school, he met a man lying fallen in the snow. Feeling his body, he found him already half frozen to death. So he took off his fur robe and wrapped it around him, and carried him back to his own home, where he revived him. That night he dreamed a supernatural being told him, "You saved a man's life out of a heart of utmost sincerity. I will have Han Qi be born into your family as your son." So when Grand Historian Feng was later born, he was given the name Qi.

A Minister surnamed Ying of Taizhou Prefecture, Zhejiang, studied diligently in the mountains in the prime of his life, preparing for the examinations. At night many ghosts wailed long and short, gathering all around him, most frighteningly; but he was not afraid at all.

One night he heard a ghost say, "A certain woman — because her husband has been long away and not returned, and because her parents-in-law think their son has died abroad, are forcing her to remarry. She is resolved not to consent; tomorrow night she will hang herself here. Now I have found my substitute." Lord Ying thereupon secretly sold his own fields, received four taels of silver, and, pretending to be her husband, wrote a letter and sent it with the silver to her home. At first, seeing that the handwriting did not match, the old couple were somewhat suspicious. But then they thought, "A letter can be forged, but who would forge silver? We suppose our son is safe and sound." So they no longer pressed the daughter-in-law to remarry. Later their son returned, and the couple were not separated, living well together as before.

Lord Ying again heard the ghost say, "I had already found my substitute, but this scholar ruined my great scheme." A ghost beside him said, "Then why do you not harm him?" That ghost answered, "Because this man's heart is good, the Lord on High has already decreed that he be made a Minister of Hidden Virtue. How could I harm him!"

Because of this, Lord Ying applied himself the more diligently, strictly disciplining himself; his good accumulated day by day, and his virtue deepened day by day. Whenever there was a famine year, he always contributed grain from his own household to relieve the starving. When relatives were in acute difficulty, he always thought of every means to help them through. When he met unreasonable words and deeds, he always sought the cause within himself, accepting them calmly and without dispute. His descendants who passed the examinations are many down to this day.

Xu Shi of Changshu County, Jiangsu, had the style name Fengzhu. His father had always been wealthy; whenever there was a famine year, he was always the first to remit rents, setting an example for the whole county, and he also took out a portion of his own grain to relieve the poor families.

At night he heard ghosts singing at his door: "Never false, never false — the Xu family scholar has become a provincial graduate." The calls went on ceaselessly all through the night. That year Xu Fengzhu indeed passed the provincial examination. His father therefore accumulated virtue all the more, diligently doing good without the least slack — repairing bridges and roads, feeding monks and helping the multitudes; and to every matter that could benefit people he gave his whole heart.
Later he again heard ghosts singing at his door: "Never false, never false — the Xu family graduate rises straight to the chief tribunal." Xu Fengzhu's office indeed rose to Governor of the Two Zhe.

Tu Kangxi of Jiaxing Prefecture was at first a Secretary in the Ministry of Justice. At night he lodged in the prison and questioned each prisoner condemned to death in detail about the circumstances of his case, discovering a number of the innocent. But Lord Tu did not claim the credit for himself; rather, he secretly wrote these circumstances into a memorial and reported it to the Minister of Justice. Later, when the death sentences were re-examined, the Minister of Justice used the words of the memorial to examine these prisoners — none did not submit — and because of it released over ten people who had been wrongfully accused and had confessed under torture. For a time the whole capital praised the Minister of Justice's sagacity.

Lord Tu also reported to the Minister of Justice, saying, "Beneath the feet of the Son of Heaven, in the capital itself, there are still so many wronged people; across a country this vast, with people in their tens of millions, how could there be none who are wronged? There should be, once every five years, a commission of officers to reduce sentences sent to each province to verify the cases and rectify the unjust imprisonments." The Minister of Justice presented Lord Tu's proposal to the court, and it was approved. At that time Lord Tu himself was one of the commissioned officers sent to reduce sentences.

That night he dreamed a supernatural being told him, "Your destiny has no son. Now your proposal to reduce sentences accords deeply with Heaven's mind; the Lord of Heaven grants you three sons, who in the future will all become great officials." That very night Lord Tu's wife became pregnant, and later she bore three sons: Yingxun, Yingkun, and Yingling, all of whom became eminent high officials.

Bao Ping of Jiaxing County, whose courtesy name was Xinzhi — his father was the Prefect of Chiyang Prefecture. He had seven sons, and Bao Ping was the youngest; he was taken as a son-in-law into the Yuan family of Pinghu County, and his friendship with my father was very deep, with frequent visits between them. His learning was broad and his talent overflowing, yet he took the provincial examinations several times without passing, and in ordinary times he liked to study Buddhism and Daoism.

One day he roamed east to Mao Lake, and chanced upon a temple in a village. Seeing the image of Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva wet all over, he immediately opened his bag, took out ten taels of silver, and gave them to the presiding monk, asking him to repair the dilapidated and leaking halls. The monk told him, "The work is great; ten taels is too little; it cannot be completed." Bao Ping further took out four bolts of cloth produced in Songjiang, and from his bamboo trunk took out seven garments, and gave them to the monk. Among them the hemp-lined jacket had been newly made on this visit to Songjiang Prefecture, and his servant urged him to stop. Bao Ping said, "If only I can make the sacred image secure — what does it matter if I go naked and bare-bodied?" The monk was moved to tears and said, "Giving silver, cloth, and garments is not so hard; but this heart of utmost sincerity of yours — that is truly most difficult!"

Later, when the halls were repaired, Bao Ping took his father to tour them, and stayed the night in the temple. He dreamed that the Dharma-protecting spirit came to thank him, saying, "Your son will enjoy the blessing of holding office for generations." Later his son Bao Bian and his grandson Bao Chengfang both passed the highest examinations and became eminent high officials.

In Jiashan County, Zhejiang, there was a man named Zhi Li. His father, Lord Zhi, was a clerk in charge of criminal matters. A prisoner, falsely accused by others and sentenced to death, was greatly pitied by Lord Zhi, who sought a way to save him. This prisoner said to his wife, "Lord Zhi's kindness — I am ashamed that I have no way to repay it. Tomorrow invite him to the countryside; if you give yourself to serve him, perhaps he will do his utmost to exonerate me, and then I can live." His wife agreed, weeping. When Lord Zhi arrived, the prisoner's wife came out in person to offer him drink and told Lord Zhi all her husband's intention. Lord Zhi would not hear of it at all, and continued to do his utmost to clear her husband, and at last rectified this unjust case.

When this prisoner was released from prison, husband and wife came to his door to kowtow their thanks, saying, "Your great virtue like this is rare in recent ages. You have no son as yet; I wish to give you my little daughter as a concubine to sweep the floor. This is proper and in accord with ritual." Lord Zhi then prepared the betrothal gifts and formally married their daughter, and so Zhi Li was born. At twenty, Zhi Li went to take the provincial examination and passed as one of the top five — the Classic Exemplar — and later served in the Hanlin Academy in the post of secretary. Zhi Li begot Zhi Gao; Zhi Gao begot Zhi Lu, who were both selected as instructors in the prefectural and county schools. Zhi Lu's son, Zhi Dalun, passed the highest examination.

The ten examples given above, though they do different things, when summed up are all a single word: "good." If we speak more precisely, good has true and false, upright and crooked, hidden and manifested, right and wrong, partial and correct, half and full, great and small, difficult and easy — all of these should be clearly distinguished. If one does good without understanding the principle, and so thinks one has been doing good all along, one is in fact accumulating evil — wasting all one's pains to no benefit at all.

What is called true good and false good? In the past, several scholars went to pay their respects to Dhyana Master Zhongfeng. They asked, "Buddhists say that the retribution of good and evil follows one like a shadow follows its form. Now here is a certain man who is good, yet his descendants do not flourish; another man is evil, yet his family is prosperous. If so, the Buddha's words have no basis!"

Dhyana Master Zhongfeng said, "Ordinary people have not washed away their worldly feelings and lack right knowledge and right views, and so take good for evil and call evil good — this happens often. They do not repent their own inversion of right and wrong; how can they instead blame Heaven for a mistaken retribution?" The crowd said, "Good is good and evil is evil — how could they possibly be inverted?" Dhyana Master Zhongfeng then asked them to try to set forth the circumstances of doing good and doing evil. One man said, "Scolding and beating others is evil; respecting and treating others with propriety is good." Dhyana Master Zhongfeng said, "Not necessarily." Another said, "Coveting wealth and demanding money greedily is evil; being incorruptible and principled is good." Dhyana Master Zhongfeng said, "Not necessarily." The crowd then related one after another the things they had seen and heard, of "doing good and meeting calamity, doing evil and gaining blessing." Dhyana Master Zhongfeng said they were all mistaken — calling evil good and taking good for evil.

Thereupon they asked Dhyana Master Zhongfeng: just what is good and what is evil? Dhyana Master Zhongfeng told them, "To benefit others is good; to benefit oneself is evil. If it benefits others, then beating and scolding are good. If it benefits oneself, then respecting and treating others with propriety are evil. Therefore, when a person does good, what benefits others is public, and the public is true good; what benefits oneself is private, and the private is false good. Moreover, what comes forth from the heart is true good; what is done for show is false good. Doing good without any seeking is true good; doing good with some seeking is false good. All of these one should examine and distinguish carefully oneself."

What is called upright good and crooked good? Now when people see a cautious, compliant goody-goody, most call him a good person and like him. But the sage would rather choose those who are bold in advancing and untrammeled by petty formalities, considering them good persons, because they dare to act and dare to take responsibility. As for the goody-goody, though the whole village likes him, he is in truth a thief of the morals of the age and the people, because he has no principles and drifts with the current; and under his influence the morals of the age and the people are ruined without anyone being aware. This shows that the criteria of good and evil of the world are plainly the opposite of those of the sage.

Following this out, the standards of taking and rejecting of the worldly are all absurd and inverted. Yet the standard by which Heaven, Earth, ghosts, and spirits bless good and punish evil is the same as the sage's, and does not comply with the views of the world. Therefore, whoever wishes to accumulate good must by no means bend to the talk and views of the world, but must, from the depths of the mind, silently wash and purify, remove selfishness and desires, and act according to the sage's standard of good and evil.

To do good out of a pure heart of benefiting the world is upright good; if there is the slightest heart of pleasing the world, it is crooked good. To do good out of a pure heart of loving others is upright good; if there is any heart of resentment toward the world, it is crooked good. To do good out of a pure heart of respecting others is upright good; if there is any heart of trifling with the world, it is crooked good. All should be carefully distinguished.

What is called hidden good and manifest good? Whenever good is done and known to others, it is manifest good; when good is done and not known to others, it is hidden virtue. Hidden virtue, Heaven repays with blessing; manifest good enjoys the praise of the world, and praise is also a blessing.

Fame is what Heaven envies and loathes. Those in the world who enjoy a great reputation not matching their substance are mostly visited with strange calamities; those who persist in doing good despite naked slander, their descendants often suddenly flourish. Between hidden virtue and manifest good the retribution is indeed most subtle. What is called right good and wrong good? The law of the state of Lu provided that if anyone paid money to redeem the common people who had been taken captive in war by enemy states and made slaves or maidservants, restoring them to freedom, the government would, according to the regulation, give a sum of money as reward. Confucius' disciple Zigong redeemed these slaves and servants but did not accept the government's reward. Hearing this, Confucius said angrily, "Zigong is wrong! The sage in his dealings can transform customs and inculcate good, serving as a model for the multitude to teach the people, and should not seek only his own satisfaction. Now in Lu the rich are few and the poor many; Zigong's act is as if to tell the multitude that to accept the government's reward is to be greedy for wealth, and so he was unwilling to accept. In this way everyone will fear the ill name of greed — how then will anyone go to redeem people? From now on, no one will go to the nobles to redeem people."

Confucius' disciple Zilu rescued a man from the water. The man gave him an ox in gratitude, and Zilu accepted it. Confucius, hearing of it, said joyfully, "Henceforth the people of Lu who are brave in rescuing others from the water will be more and more numerous!" Because Zilu and the man who gave the ox set up a good model: the one brave in rescuing from peril, the other generous in repaying virtue. In this way a good social atmosphere will be formed.

From the worldly point of view, Zigong's not accepting the reward was good, and Zilu's accepting the ox was not good. But Confucius praised Zilu and condemned Zigong. This shows that the sage's views often differ from the world's. We should emulate the sage, and then we will accord with Heaven's mind.

Thereupon one knows: in a person's doing good, one does not look at the present moment but at whether it has harmful consequences; not at one time but at the long run; not at one person but at the whole world. What appears now to be a good deed, but when it spreads abroad is enough to harm people, is like good yet in fact not good; what appears now to be not good, but when it spreads abroad is enough to help people, is like not good yet in fact good.

However, here we have discussed only this one matter of "the good that is not good." Others, such as the righteousness that is not righteousness, the propriety that is not propriety, the trustworthiness that is not trustworthiness, the kindness that is not kindness — all should be distinguished and chosen.

What is called partial and correct? In the past, when Lord Lu Wenyi had just resigned from the post of Grand Chancellor and returned to his hometown, the whole nation regarded him with great esteem. A man of the village, drunk, came before Lord Lu's residence and cursed him loudly. Lord Lu was not angry, and said to his servant, "A drunken man — do not contend with him. Shut the gate and pay him no heed."

A year passed, and this man committed a capital crime and was imprisoned. Only then did Lord Lu regret it, saying, "If at the time I had contended with him a little, sent him to the yamen to be punished, then through this small punishment I could have greatly warned him. At the time I only thought of being kind-hearted and letting him go, not realizing I was fostering his arrogance and evil, until finally he committed a capital crime!" This is an example of doing an evil deed with a good heart.

There is also doing a good deed with an evil heart. For example, in a famine year, a great wealthy household saw the poor people robbing food in the streets in broad daylight. He reported it to the county, but the magistrate, fearing trouble, ignored it, and the poor became ever more audacious. Thereupon this wealthy household privately sent people to seize the robbers and imprison them, and expose their shame; only then did the poor settle down. Otherwise the market would have fallen into disorder.

Therefore, good is correct and evil is partial — this everyone knows. Those who do evil deeds with a good heart, like Lord Lu mentioned above, are the partial within the correct; those who do good deeds with an evil heart, like the wealthy household mentioned above, are the correct within the partial. This everyone must know.

What is called half good and full good? The Classic of Changes says, "If good is not accumulated, it is not enough to establish a name; if evil is not accumulated, it is not enough to bring the disaster of death." The Book of History says, "The evil of the Shang dynasty, accumulated one thing after another, has now filled up." Accumulating good is likewise like putting things into a container: if one puts them in diligently and constantly, it soon fills; if one is slack and does not accumulate, it will not fill. This is one account of half good and full good.

In the past, a woman came to a temple wishing to make an offering, but had not much money; she took out the two coppers she had on her and offered them. To her surprise, the abbot came in person to repent on her behalf of her karmic hindrances. Later she entered the palace, became wealthy and honored, and took several thousand taels of silver to offer at this temple, but the abbot only had his disciples turn the merit back for her. Completely bewildered, she asked, "The last time I offered only two coppers, and you repented in person for me; now I offer several thousand taels of silver, and you do not turn the merit for me. Why?" The abbot replied, "The last time, though your money was little, your heart was extremely sincere; if I had not repented in person for you, it would not have been enough to repay your merit. Now, though your money is great, your heart is not as sincere as before; I have others do the repenting on your behalf, and that suffices." Therefore, if the heart is not sincere, a thousand gold is but half good; if the heart is sincere, two coppers are full good.

Zhongli handed the elixir to Master Lü, which could turn iron into gold, to be used to save the world. Master Lü asked, "This gold is transformed from iron; in the end will it change back?" Zhongli replied, "After five hundred years it will revert to iron." Master Lü said, "To be able to turn iron to gold is indeed quite remarkable and could help many people, but it would bitterly harm the people of five hundred years hence; I am unwilling to do it." Zhongli said, "Cultivating immortality requires accumulating three thousand good deeds, but this one sentence of yours has already fulfilled those three thousand good deeds." This is another account of half good and full good.

Moreover, if one does good and does not keep the deed in the mind, then whatever good is done, great or small, is full good; if one keeps the deed in the mind, though one does it diligently all one's life, one only attains half good.

For example, when using wealth to help others, if within one does not see oneself, without one does not see the recipient, and between one does not see the wealth given — this is the emptiness of the three wheels, this is single-minded purity. Doing thus, one bushel of grain can plant boundless, measureless blessing, and one copper can wipe away the offenses of a thousand kalpas. If in the mind one still recollects that I gave wealth to such a one and I did such a good deed, then though one uses ten thousand taels of gold, it is only half good, and the blessing planted is not full. This is yet another account of half good and full good.

What is called great good and small good? In the past, when Wei Zhongda was serving in the Hanlin Academy, his soul was summoned to the underworld. The official in charge ordered the clerk to present the two records of his good and evil. When the records arrived, the evil record actually filled the whole hall, while the good record was only a small thin roll, like a single chopstick. The official ordered a scale to weigh them; the evil record filling the hall was in fact light, while that roll as thin as a chopstick was in fact heavy.

Zhongda asked, "I am not yet past forty; how can my faults and evils be so many?" The official replied, "A single thought not upright is a fault or evil; it does not wait until you actually commit it." Zhongda then asked again, "What is written in that small roll?" The official said, "Once the emperor wished to undertake a great project, building the Three Mountains stone bridge in Fujian Prefecture. You feared it would weary the people and waste money, and so you submitted a memorial to dissuade him. This is the draft of that memorial."

Zhongda said, "Though I submitted the memorial, the court did not heed it, and it did no good; how could it have such great power of good?" The official replied, "Though the court did not heed it, your single thought was already for the myriad people; had it been heeded, the power of good would be even greater." Therefore, if a good deed is for the sake of the people of the world and the state, then though the matter is small, its merit is great; if it is for the sake of a single individual, then though the matter is great, its merit is small.

What is called difficult and easy? In the past the former sages said, "To restrain one's selfish desires and control one's conduct, one must begin where it is difficult to restrain and difficult to control, and keep on restraining and controlling."

One must be like the venerable Mr. Shu of Jiangxi Province. Teaching in another place, on the road home he met a woman weeping bitterly, because her husband, in debt to the government for silver, was forced to sell his wife. He gave all the salary he had earned in two years of hard work to pay on her behalf, so that the couple were not separated. One must also be like the Elder Zhang of Handan County. He saved money in a jar, and only after ten years was it full. A neighbor had to sell his wife to pay for a crime, and his three children were still young. Elder Zhang, fearing that after she left the three children could not be raised, and that the woman could hardly live, gave all the money he had saved over ten years to pay the redemption silver on their behalf, saving the mother and her four. These are the cases of being able to give up where it is hard to give up.

Another is the Elder Jin of Zhenjiang Prefecture. At fifty, with no son, his wife sold her ornaments to buy the neighbor's daughter to be his concubine, hoping she would bear him a son. When Elder Jin returned home and discovered this, unable to bear to marry so young a woman, he immediately sent her back to the neighbor. This is being able to endure where it is hard to endure.
Because they could give up at the hard-to-give-up and endure at the hard-to-endure, so the blessings Heaven bestowed upon them were likewise very deep.

For those with wealth and power, to establish merit and virtue is everywhere very easy; to be easy and yet not do it is to waste oneself. For the poor and lowly, to do good and cultivate blessing is everywhere very hard; to be hard and yet able to do it — this is truly most precious.

Doing good is according with conditions to rescue the many, and so its kinds are extremely numerous. Summed up, there are roughly ten categories: first, being good with others; second, keeping a mind of love and respect; third, helping others perfect their good; fourth, urging others to do good; fifth, rescuing others in peril; sixth, building the great benefit; seventh, giving wealth to create blessing; eighth, upholding the true Dharma; ninth, honoring and respecting elders and superiors; tenth, cherishing the lives of beings.

What is called being good with others? In the past, Shun, by the shore of Thunder Lake, saw that the young and strong fishermen all took the deep pools and eddies rich in fish, while the old and weak could only fish at the rapids and shallows, and of course caught no fish. Shun's heart could not bear it; pitying these old and weak ones, he too went fishing. When Shun saw those who contended for the spots, he avoided speaking of their faults; when he saw those who yielded, he praised them everywhere and emulated them. After a year, everyone was yielding to one another the deep pools and confluences.

With Shun's bright and penetrating wisdom, how could he not have spoken a discourse to instruct everyone? The reason he did not use words, but through the example of his own conduct gently transformed the hearts of people and the manners of the age — this is precisely the painstaking care of a master craftsman's design!
